articles.title: Ranking Member Maxine Waters and Committee Democrats Blast SEC Push to Eliminate Climate Risk Disclosures - U.S. House Committee on Financial Services Democrats (.gov)
articles.summary: Ranking Member Maxine Waters and Committee Democrats Blast SEC Push to Eliminate Climate Risk Disclosures  U.S. House Committee on Financial Services Democrats (.gov)

source_detail.name: U.S. House Committee on Financial Services Democrats (.gov)

articles.full_text:
Today, Congresswoman Maxine Waters (D-CA), the top Democrat on the House Financial Services Committee, along with Representatives Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), Juan Vargas (D-CA), Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), Nikema Williams (D-GA) and Sam Liccardo (D-CA), sent a letter to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chairman Paul S. Atkins strongly opposing the Commission’s proposal to eliminate the March 2024 climate-related disclosure rules.
In the letter, the lawmakers warn that eliminating the rules would deprive investors of critical information about the financial risks companies face from climate change at a time when climate-related events are becoming increasingly more common and disruptive to businesses and the broader economy. They argue that the SEC has a responsibility to ensure investors have consistent, standardized information necessary to evaluate these risks and make informed decisions with their money.
“Stripping away these rules denies investors the information they need to accurately assess a company’s long-term value and to make sound, well-informed decisions with their hard-earned money,” the lawmakers wrote.
The lawmakers also dispute the Commission’s argument that the SEC exceeded its statutory authority in adopting the rules. They point to the SEC’s longstanding authority under federal securities laws to determine what information public companies must disclose to investors, as well as the Commission’s decades-long history of requiring disclosures in response to evolving market risks and economic conditions. The letter notes that the SEC has required various forms of environmental disclosure dating back to the 1970s and argues that climate-related disclosures fall within the Commission’s traditional role of ensuring investors have relevant information when making investment decisions.
The lawmakers added, “…nothing in the governing statutes, case law, or legislative history has changed since March 2024, and Congress has amended neither the Securities Act nor the Exchange Act. The only thing that has changed is the composition of the Commission.”
The letter also pushes back on arguments that climate disclosures are unnecessary or immaterial to investors. The lawmakers point to data showing that companies actively managing climate risks can realize significant financial benefits, while 80 percent of investors want the opportunity to invest in companies that consider environmental sustainability. Investors and financial institutions representing hundreds of trillions of dollars in assets have also sought climate-related information from companies to inform their investment and financing decisions.
The lawmakers conclude by urging the Commission to maintain the existing disclosure framework and withdraw its proposal to rescind the rules.
Full list of signers includes: Nydia Velázquez (D-NY), Brad Sherman (D-CA), Gregory Meeks (D-NY), Stephen Lynch (D-MA), Al Green (D-TX), Emanuel Cleaver (D-MO), Bill Foster (D-IL), Joyce Beatty (D-OH), Juan Vargas (D-CA), Ayanna Pressley (D-MA), Rashida Tlaib (D-MI), Ritchie Torres (D-NY), Sylvia Garcia (D-TX), Nikema Williams (D-GA), Sam Liccardo (D-CA).
Read the full letter HERE.
Background:
    - June 16, 2021 — Passed climate-risk disclosure legislation through the House. Then Chairwoman Waters led House passage of a broader ESG disclosure package, which would require public companies to disclose financial and business risks associated with climate change. Read Waters' floor statement on passage of the legislation. 
- March 21, 2022 — Applauded the SEC's proposed climate-disclosure rule after years of Committee action. Then-Chairwoman Waters joined committee Dems in a letter to commending the SEC's proposed rule requiring climate-related disclosures by public companies. Waters highlighted that, under her leadership, the Committee had already held four hearings on the issue and advanced legislation from Committee Democrats over the previous two Congresses. Read Waters and Committee Dems statement on the proposed SEC rule. 
- October 6, 2023 — Pressed SEC Chair Gary Gensler to quickly finalize the rule. Waters urged Gensler to finish the long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule, warning that climate change and transition risks threatened Americans' investments, retirement savings, businesses and broader financial stability. She argued that investors needed consistent and comparable information to understand those risks. Read Waters' letter urging Gensler to finalize the climate-risk disclosure rule. 
- March 7, 2024 — Supported the SEC's final climate-disclosure rule while pushing for stronger protections. After the SEC finalized the rule, Waters welcomed the creation of standardized climate-risk disclosures but criticized the Commission for significantly weakening its original proposal. She specifically raised concerns about the treatment of Scope 1 and 2 emissions and the elimination of Scope 3 requirements, while emphasizing the real financial consequences of climate change for investors, homeowners and renters. Read Waters' statement on the final SEC climate-disclosure rule.
- April 10, 2024 — Defended the climate rule against Republican attacks in a full Committee hearing. At a Republican-led hearing titled “Beyond Scope: How the SEC's Climate Rule Threatens American Markets,” Waters defended the rule as a commonsense investor protection, arguing that climate change affects companies' financial health and investors have a right to understand how the companies they own are responding to those risks. Read Waters' opening statement defending the SEC climate rule. 
- June 5, 2024 — Led 36 lawmakers with Senator Elizabeth Warren in pressing the SEC to defend and enforce the rule. Waters and Warren led 36 lawmakers urging the SEC to remain focused on climate risk despite litigation challenging the rule. They called on the Commission to enforce its existing climate-risk guidance while the rule was stayed, use every available resource to defend the rule in court and robustly implement it once the stay was lifted. Read the Waters-Warren letter and Committee release. 
- September 17–19, 2024 — Fought Republican legislation restricting the SEC's disclosure authority. Waters opposed H.R. 4790, warning that it would restrict the SEC's authority to determine what information public companies must disclose, including environmental and climate-related information, and undermine investors' access to information about the companies they own. She testified against the legislation before the Rules Committee on September 17 and opposed it again on the House floor on September 19. Read Waters' September 17 testimony against H.R. 4790. Read Waters' September 19 floor statement. 
- December 29, 2025 — Demanded SEC oversight after Chairman Paul Atkins abandoned the climate-rule defense. Waters called for a long-overdue oversight hearing with Atkins amid sweeping changes at the SEC, including the Commission's retreat from climate-risk disclosure. The request put the Administration's reversal of climate-related investor protections squarely within the Committee Democrats' broader oversight of Atkins' leadership. Read Waters' request for an SEC oversight hearing. 
- February 11, 2026 — Confronted Atkins directly over halting the SEC's defense of the climate rule. When Atkins finally appeared before the Committee, Waters criticized his SEC for having “halted the SEC's defense of the climate disclosure rule” even as the California wildfires demonstrated the material financial risks associated with climate change. She placed the decision within a broader critique that Atkins' SEC was prioritizing Wall Street and billionaires over investors. Read Waters' February 2026 opening statement confronting Atkins.

articles.title: ESG Focus: UK/EU/International ESG Regulation Monthly Round-Up – August/September 2026 - www.hlc.com
articles.summary: ESG Focus: UK/EU/International ESG Regulation Monthly Round-Up – August/September 2026  www.hlc.com
articles.full_text:
Panoramic: Automotive and Mobility 2026
We took a brief summer break but are back with this edition of the ESG Regulation Monthly Round-Up covering developments from the UK, EU and internationally during August and September 2026.
Generally there have been a lot of developments around corporate sustainability reporting in the UK, EU, Australia, New Zealand and California. The direction of travel seems to be a recalibration of mandatory expectations on companies. There have also been a number of conversations and plans announced around adaptation and resilience – which is a leading topic as we head to the end of 2026.
In this issue:
Chapter 3: International developments
In the UK there have been a number of corporate sustainability reporting updates, the direction of travel seems to be simplification and modernisation of reporting. We have also seen an update in the UK ETS and UK Financial Conduct Authority (“FCA”) focus on adaptation, perhaps recognising the extreme heat this summer in the UK and the EU and the publication of the “A Well-Adapted UK” report.
a. UK corporate reporting updates
- FCA published Policy Statement (PS26/19): Aligning listed issuers’ sustainability disclosures with international standards: The FCA has confirmed that UK SRS will be adopted maintaining the “comply or explain” approach. These new rules will replace the TCFD-aligned disclosures for UK-listed issuers. The rules will apply to accounting periods beginning on 1 January 2027, with first reporting in 2028 and some transitional reliefs applicable. Read more here.
- FCA confirmed simplifications to TCFD-aligned disclosures for asset managers and asset owners: On 25 September 2026, the FCA published Handbook Notice No 144 which simplifies product-level climate disclosure requirements for asset managers, life insurers and FCA-regulated pension providers. The changes introduce more targeted disclosure rules intended to reduce complexity while improving the clarity and usability of climate information for retail and institutional investors. The rules came into force on 25 September 2026. Read more here.
- Modernising corporate reporting: On 7 September 2026, the UK Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (“BIST”) published an open consultation seeking views on how the corporate reporting framework in the UK could be modernised to better meet the needs of companies, investors and the wider economy. The consultation closes on 30 November 2026. Read more here.
b. UK ETS – consultation on free allocation rules for hydrogen production opens
On 7 September 2026, the Department for Energy Security & Net Zero (DESNZ) updated its UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) policy webpage to reflect that a new consultation on free allocation rules for hydrogen production – targeted technical consultation has opened. It closes on 2 October 2026.
c. UK FCA publishes web page on climate adaptation and resilience
On 4 August 2026, the UK Financial Conduct Authority (“FCA”) published a new web page providing information for regulated firms on how physical risks from climate change may impact the property insurance and mortgage markets. It sets out the risks it has identified and sets out their work so far on insurance, mortgage lending and the Climate Financial Risk Forum.
With this focus on adaptation and resilience, it is likely that the FCA will update more policies on insurance, mortgage lending and climate risk management leading to additional requirements on financial institutions. This is an ongoing piece of work which ties into firms general need to ensure that they are up to date on climate risk assessment and understand adaptation, risk management and data on climate-related risks to properties.
In the EU this month, the EmpCo Directive became applicable to businesses making B2C environmental and social claims, final ESRS and VESRS were published and other updates included developments on EU ETS, adaptation and resilience and SFDR 2.0.
a. EmpCo Directive comes applicable from 27 September 2026
Following entry into force on 26 March 2024, Member States have been busy transposing the EU Directive on Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition (the “EmpCo Directive”, also known as the ECGT Directive) into national law. The EmpCo Directive applies from 27 September 2026 and amends existing directives to (i) ban greenwashing and misleading product information and (ii) enhance consumers’ rights to better information, improved product labelling and more visible guarantees. Read more here and here.
b. EU corporate sustainability reporting: simplified ESRS and VESRS published in Official Journal
On 21 September 2026, the final revised and simplified European Sustainability Reporting Standards (“ESRS”) and the sustainability reporting standard for voluntary use (“VESRS”) were published in the Official Journal of the European Union.
The publication of the simplified ESRS and the VESRS follows the EU adoption of the omnibus simplification package and a lengthy process to “simplify” and “reduce administrative burden” for EU businesses whilst maintaining high quality sustainability disclosures. As part of the omnibus process, the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (“CSRD”) was amended to raise, amongst other things, the financial thresholds for compliance with the CSRD reducing the number of companies falling in scope for compliance (though these amendments will need to be transposed by each Member State). Read more about the updated scope of the CSRD here.
In addition, on 28 August 2026, EFRAG published its new draft 2026 list of datapoints for the revised ESRS. The list brings together the definitions of the ESRS datapoints to support undertakings preparing sustainability statements in accordance with the revised standards.
c. EU Emissions Trading System (“EU ETS”) – summary and briefing paper
On 16 September 2026, the European Parliament published an EU briefing summarising the Commission’s proposals to revise the EU ETS and next steps.
The Legislative Train confirms that the Parliament has referred the proposal to the Committee on Environment, Climate and Food Safety (ENVI) and aims to have a position ready by the end of the year. The environment ministers of the Council intend to hold a policy debate on 12 October 2026, adopting an Environment Council general approach on 11 December 2026. The Parliament and Council are targeting an agreement in the first quarter of 2027.
d. EU State of the Union speech – climate, adaptation and insurance
On 16 September 2026, Ursula Von der Leyen gave the annual State of the Union address to the European Union confirming that the EU needs both climate change mitigation and adaptation, reflecting on the extreme temperatures, wildfires and droughts affecting many of Europe’s members.
She confirmed that the climate resilience package (previously consulted upon) is expected next month (November) and a European Heatwave Plan and European Water Initiative will be unveiled soon. This will set out a whole of society approach “all the way through to the local level where adaptation matters most”, aiming to make Europe a champion of adaptation technologies.
She also confirmed that the Commission will make proposals to improve risk management and address the insurance gap, setting up a Climate Insurance Alliance.
These are also set out in a letter to the Presidency.
e. SFDR 2.0 update: MEPs vote for clearer, simpler sustainable finance disclosure rules
On 10 September 2026, the European Parliament published a press release confirming that the Economic and Monetary Affairs Committee (ECON) has adopted a text for SFDR 2.0.
Some of the highlights from the press release were:
- MEPs support the three standard product categories (sustainable, transition, and ESG basics).
- Transition products channelling investments towards fossil fuel companies (unless such companies invest heavily in environmentally sustainable activities) should have “a measurable, time-bound plan to cut emissions, and put more capital into sustainable activities than into new fossil fuel projects”.
- Products falling under ESG basics category (Environmental, Social, Governance) should also disclose their exposure to the fossil fuel sector. All three categories should exclude investments in companies violating human rights and humanitarian law.
- MEPs agreed to exempt professional investors, and to remove financial advice and portfolio management from the rules' scope.
We can expect to see the negotiating mandate of the Parliament announced at the start of October and after that the final legislation still needs to be agreed with the Council before coming into force.
f. Commission publishes guidelines on the application of the EU Forced Labour Regulation
On 3 September 2026, the European Commission published Guidelines of the application of the EU Forced Labour Regulation to support the implementation of the regulation. They are addressed to competent authorities responsible for implementing the Regulation and to customs authorities, economic operators, consumer associations, civil society organisations, trade unions and any other stakeholders.
g. Commission updates the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (“PPWR”) FAQ
The first wave of obligations under the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (EU) 2025/40 applied from 12 August 2026. Just before that date, the Commission published the second edition of its Frequently Asked Questions document (“FAQ”).
The updated FAQ goes beyond further details on topics already addressed in the first edition: It gives a clearer indication of the Commission’s understanding of PPWR obligations, including on aspects where national registers and enforcement authorities had previously sent different signals.

articles.title: Thailand Raises $750 Million in Asia-Pacific’s First Sovereign Nature-Linked Bond
articles.summary:
The Government of Thailand has raised approximately $750 million through a sovereign sustainability-linked bond that ties public financing directly to climate and biodiversity targets. The 15-year bond, issued on September […]
The post Thailand Raises $750 Million in Asia-Pacific’s First Sovereign Nature-Linked Bond appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Thailand Raises $750 Million in Asia-Pacific’s First Sovereign Nature-Linked Bond
- Thailand raised approximately $750 million through a 15-year sustainability-linked sovereign bond tied to both emissions reduction and nature conservation targets.
- The bond introduces Asia-Pacific’s first sovereign sustainability-linked structure incorporating a nature-related performance indicator.
- Investor subscriptions reached 2.8 times the initially planned issuance, highlighting demand for sovereign debt linked to measurable climate and biodiversity outcomes.
The Government of Thailand has raised approximately $750 million through a sovereign sustainability-linked bond that ties public financing directly to climate and biodiversity targets.
The 15-year bond, issued on September 17 with support from the Asian Development Bank (ADB), raised $750 million. It is the first sovereign sustainability-linked bond in Asia and the Pacific to incorporate a nature-related performance indicator.
The transaction builds on Thailand’s inaugural sustainability-linked sovereign bond issuance in 2024. This latest structure adds a biodiversity-focused KPI and strengthens the environmental targets attached to the financing.
Climate and nature targets enter sovereign debt
Thailand has linked the bond to two sustainability objectives aligned with its national environmental priorities and international commitments.
The first is to keep the country’s net greenhouse gas emissions below 152 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent by 2035. That would represent a 47% reduction from 2019 levels.
The second target focuses directly on nature. Thailand aims to conserve and manage at least 30% of its terrestrial and inland water areas by 2030. The target covers protected areas and other effective area-based conservation measures.
Bringing biodiversity into a sovereign sustainability-linked structure expands the use of capital markets beyond conventional climate metrics. Nature loss is increasingly becoming a financial and governance issue for governments, companies and investors.
“This landmark transaction demonstrates how capital markets can help deliver mitigation and biodiversity outcomes,” said ADB Country Director for Thailand Aaron Batten. “We congratulate the Government of Thailand on this landmark achievement, which further strengthens the country’s position as a leader in sustainable finance. The issuance aligns with ADB’s commitment to mobilize $30 billion through capital markets by 2030 and provides a valuable model for other countries seeking to mobilize investment and translate their mitigation and biodiversity commitments into measurable outcomes.”
Investor demand exceeds planned issuance
Demand substantially exceeded Thailand’s original fundraising plan. Investor subscriptions reached 2.8 times the planned issue amount of $450 million.
The government ultimately raised 25 billion baht, pointing to strong appetite among domestic and international investors for sustainability-linked sovereign instruments.
Unlike traditional use-of-proceeds green bonds, sustainability-linked instruments connect financing terms to predefined performance targets. That structure places greater emphasis on credible KPIs, measurement and accountability.
For sovereign issuers, it also creates another mechanism for translating national climate and biodiversity commitments into financial market structures.
ADB helped Thailand select the indicators, coordinate participating partners and review the bond framework against international standards.
RELATED ARTICLE: Asian Development Bank Commits Half of its Lending to Climate Finance by 2030
Regional sustainable finance infrastructure expands
ADB provided its support through technical assistance under the Green Social Sustainability and Other-labeled Finance Initiative, known as GSS+.
The initiative combines the ASEAN Catalytic Green Finance Facility (ACGF) with the Asian Bond Markets Initiative (ABMI). Thailand also received support through ADB’s Nature Solutions Finance Hub, which aims to expand nature-positive investment across the region.
ACGF operates through the ASEAN Infrastructure Fund and focuses on accelerating green infrastructure investment in Southeast Asia. ABMI brings together ASEAN governments alongside China, Japan and South Korea to develop local currency bond markets.
The institutional backing matters as Asian governments face growing pressure to finance climate adaptation, decarbonization and ecosystem protection without relying exclusively on public budgets.
What investors and executives should watch
Thailand’s issuance broadens the sovereign sustainable finance market by placing biodiversity alongside emissions as a measurable financing consideration.
For investors, the transaction offers another example of how nature-related targets can enter mainstream fixed-income structures. It also raises the importance of credible measurement, reporting and governance around biodiversity commitments.
For governments, Thailand provides a potential template for connecting national environmental targets with capital market access.
That could become increasingly relevant as countries work to fund both Paris Agreement commitments and the global goal of conserving 30% of land and water by 2030.
Thailand’s bond therefore extends beyond a single sovereign financing exercise. It tests whether measurable nature outcomes can become part of the financial architecture governments use to fund their environmental commitments across Asia and beyond.

articles.title: The Blind Spot at Climate Week NYC – Why Climate Finance Needs the ‘Builders’
articles.summary:
I arrived at Climate Week NYC expecting frustration after a difficult year of political turbulence and policy delays. Instead, I encountered a surprisingly confident industry speaking fluently in the language […]
The post The Blind Spot at Climate Week NYC – Why Climate Finance Needs the ‘Builders’  appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
The Blind Spot at Climate Week NYC – Why Climate Finance Needs the ‘Builders’
I arrived at Climate Week NYC expecting frustration after a difficult year of political turbulence and policy delays. Instead, I encountered a surprisingly confident industry speaking fluently in the language of risk, security, and capital allocation. Fluency, though, is not the same as knowing the ground you are standing on. 
Every map carries a worldview, showing us what counts as a landmark and what remains invisible. I have watched sustainability and climate grow into industries, and I always took them for new maps, drawn for a world we had not reached yet.
This year, for the first time though, I noticed a dangerous blind spot, dominating the room, disguised as hope. Energy security, the most outspoken topic of the week, seemed to have become the core mission and argument of the industry’s planetary vision. Listening to global leaders through my lens as a landscape architect, a few themes kept catching my attention.
Capital vs. Nature-based Systems Realities
Finance has always been the loudest voice at Climate Week. What changed this year is what it rests on. Green transition is no longer framed as a moral duty but as economic competitiveness, energy security, and risk management. Nadia Calviño of the European Investment Bank described doubling adaptation finance to €30 billion while linking competitiveness directly with climate action. The moral argument used to be the premise and capital the instrument; now economics is the premise and the moral case has quietly left the room.
Capital behaves like water: it flows along the path of least financial resistance, seeking existing grids, clear permitting, and financial returns. But landscapes do not adjust to balance sheets. A watershed or an energy corridor cannot be rebalanced by financial engineering alone; it is defined by soil capacity, water availability, topography, local communities, and, more importantly, extreme unknowns. Continuing to treat climate capital through strictly old financial frameworks ignores physical realities on the ground. As Gary Hamel put it decades ago, you can’t use an old map to see a new land. 
What was missing from the main stage were the builders: planners, designers, engineers, and the projects themselves. They were there, scattered across local events around the city, keeping the week alive. But not where the capital decisions were being discussed. That distance is not an accident of scheduling.
The Blind Spot of AI and Efficiency: Nobody Argued for Less
I was clearly expecting artificial intelligence to enter the rooms as an argument for reduction, fewer kilometers, less material, less friction, the same result from a smaller footprint. Yet I did not hear a single argument for doing less, or for doing the same with less.
One thing worth mentioning here; fundraising for climate-specialist venture funds fell almost 40% in 2025 and this year is heading for its worst in a decade. Capital follows AI’s appetite — generation, storage, grid — not soil and water. The money is following whoever can feed the data centres, which is a different business from the one most climate ventures are in. I also asked the climate technology companies how responsibly they use AI. The answers were vague, indistinct to be honest. The same question applies to any sustainability project that promises optimisation through AI. We will need new voices to challenge this contradiction.
RELATED ARTICLE: Day 3 at Climate Week NYC: AI, Energy and Climate Delivery
Pricing Water, and What It Doesn’t Fix
The clearest moment, that made me think we might be looking at an old map, came in a session on water, where a professor described systems entering bankruptcy: rivers and reservoirs as income, groundwater and glaciers as savings being drawn down, expenses exceeding income.
It is an excellent but sad metaphor, that also marked the edge of what that room could do. The risk of describing a watershed as a balance sheet is not inaccuracy. It is that a balance sheet can be rebalanced by selling the asset, and a watershed cannot. Water bankruptcy is a soil profile, a crop choice, a settlement pattern, a season. You can price that exposure accurately, disclose it properly, hold it indefinitely, and not one field will receive water.
Resolving that is a different kind of work: making conflicting demands, hydrology, soil, ecology, human activity, coexist within the finite limits of one place. A site has a carrying capacity that capital cannot override.
When you leave the water conversation to be led by the capital market, the legitimation of water capitalization is confirmed. Which is a fundamental conflict for planetary intelligence. If a voice in that room had joined the conversation claiming health, communities, nature-based solutions and resilience in more specific ways, the whole
claim would not feel as contradictory as it did. Claiming water as a financial asset without advocating its own rights puts you in a critical position you then have to defend. That should not be what the climate industry wants.
Antalya & COP31
Which is what I will be watching for in Antalya. The arrangement is unprecedented: Turkey hosts and holds the action agenda, while Australia leads the negotiations. Whatever is remembered from COP31 will therefore be what it demonstrated, not what it negotiated.
That makes it the clearest test of everything I heard in New York. Turkey has remarkable solar and wind potential and deep engineering expertise, alongside a continued reliance on coal that sits awkwardly beside its 2053 net-zero commitment. Abundant ground, real capital interest, and nothing yet composing them. Between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, with a farming population large enough that water security is a livelihood question rather than an abstraction, the agenda is available. As in New York, whether the planners and builders are on that stage is another matter.
The confidence I found in New York is real, and it is earned after decades of work. But confidence does not by itself mark a direction. We are sailing faster with charts drawn for a sea we already know, pricing what we cannot yet compose, and calling that progress. After the pledges are tallied and the roadmaps drawn, the question is not who pays for the journey. It is whether we are still using an old map to find new land.
Enisé Derinboğaz is an NYC based landscape architect and founder of Mori. Her projects and writing explore how nature, development, and human experience intersect in the places we build.

articles.title: Norway’s Wealth Fund Commits $1.36 Billion to CIP Renewable Energy Fund
articles.summary:
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is deepening its exposure to private renewable energy infrastructure with a $1.36 billion commitment to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ sixth flagship fund, CI VI. The agreement, […]
The post Norway’s Wealth Fund Commits $1.36 Billion to CIP Renewable Energy Fund appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Norway’s Wealth Fund Commits $1.36 Billion to CIP Renewable Energy Fund
- Norges Bank Investment Management has committed $1.36 billion to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ sixth flagship renewable energy fund, CI VI.
- CI VI will target renewable generation and energy storage projects across OECD markets in North America, Western Europe and Asia Pacific.
- The investment expands a partnership that began in 2024, when the Norwegian fund committed about $1.02 billion to CIP’s previous flagship strategy.
Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM) is deepening its exposure to private renewable energy infrastructure with a $1.36 billion commitment to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ sixth flagship fund, CI VI.
The agreement, signed on October 1, expands an investment relationship established two years ago. In 2024, NBIM committed about $1.02 billion to Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners’ fifth flagship fund, CI V.
The latest allocation gives the manager of Norway’s Government Pension Fund Global further exposure to renewable infrastructure projects before they reach operation. It also channels institutional capital toward generation and storage assets across several of the world’s largest developed economies.
“CI VI allows us to keep investing in renewable energy projects at the development stage, and builds on a partnership that has worked well for the fund since 2024,” says Harald von Heyden, Global Head of Energy and Infrastructure at Norges Bank Investment Management.
Development-stage renewables remain the focus
CI VI will primarily invest in renewable energy generation and storage across OECD countries. Its geographic mandate covers North America, Western Europe and the Asia Pacific region.
For NBIM, the commitment builds its exposure to unlisted renewable energy infrastructure. The asset class offers institutional investors access to projects that are not available through listed equity markets.
Development-stage investment also carries a different risk profile from acquiring operational assets. Projects can face permitting delays, construction risks, supply chain pressures and changes in financing conditions. Grid access and regulatory frameworks can also affect timelines and returns.
At the same time, early-stage capital remains critical to expanding renewable generation and storage capacity. Institutional investors can provide the long-duration financing needed to move large infrastructure projects through development and construction.
RELATED ARTICLE: Norges Bank Investment Management sets 2030 Climate Action Plan Toward Net-Zero
NBIM expands its CIP relationship
The $1.36 billion commitment follows NBIM’s investment in CI V in 2024, creating continuity between two successive CIP flagship strategies.
Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners has built its investment model around large-scale energy infrastructure, while NBIM has gradually expanded beyond its traditional listed portfolio into unlisted assets.
NBIM is the fund management division of Norges Bank. Its direct investments in real estate and renewable energy infrastructure are made and managed through subsidiary structures established by the central bank.
The latest allocation therefore sits within a broader diversification strategy while retaining a clear infrastructure focus.
For asset owners, the repeat commitment is notable. Large institutional investors increasingly face the challenge of translating climate objectives into investments that also meet strict risk and return requirements. Private infrastructure funds can provide access to assets that directly support the buildout of lower-carbon energy systems.
What executives and investors should watch
The commitment also highlights the growing importance of energy storage alongside renewable generation. As wind and solar capacity expands, storage is becoming more important for managing intermittent supply and supporting grid reliability.
That creates a wider investment opportunity than renewable generation alone. Capital requirements now stretch across generation, batteries, transmission, grid connections and other infrastructure needed to integrate new capacity.
For governments, attracting institutional capital will depend partly on maintaining predictable permitting, energy and investment frameworks. Policy uncertainty can increase development risk and ultimately raise financing costs.
For investors, the challenge is balancing that risk against the long-term capital requirements of the energy transition.
NBIM’s latest commitment puts another $1.36 billion behind that buildout across three major developed-market regions. Its decision to return to CIP for a second flagship fund also shows how established manager relationships can become an important channel for deploying institutional capital into the next generation of global energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Ukraine Approves ESG Roadmap to Attract Reconstruction Finance
articles.summary:
Ukraine is building ESG standards into its reconstruction strategy as the government looks to attract sustainable capital and deepen alignment with the European Union. The government approved a roadmap on […]
The post Ukraine Approves ESG Roadmap to Attract Reconstruction Finance appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine Approves ESG Roadmap to Attract Reconstruction Finance
- Ukraine has approved a 2026–2028 ESG roadmap designed to align investment and financial practices with European sustainable finance standards.
- The plan includes a sustainable finance taxonomy, corporate due diligence, ESG integration into public investment and monitoring of sustainable finance flows.
- Clearer ESG rules could help international investors assess reconstruction projects, but access to capital will depend on implementation and credible corporate compliance.
Ukraine is building ESG standards into its reconstruction strategy as the government looks to attract sustainable capital and deepen alignment with the European Union.
The government approved a roadmap on September 30 to introduce environmental, social and governance principles across investment and financial practices. The framework covers 2026 to 2028 and sets out regulatory and institutional priorities for the coming years.
For Ukraine, the stakes extend well beyond corporate sustainability reporting. Rebuilding the country will require substantial private and public capital. Investors will need credible frameworks to assess which projects qualify as sustainable and how companies manage environmental and social risks.
The roadmap is intended to provide that foundation.
Building a Ukrainian sustainable finance taxonomy
A central element of the plan is the development of a taxonomy for sustainable economic activities.
The classification system would establish clearer definitions for investments that meet sustainability criteria. This could give companies, financial institutions and international investors a more consistent basis for evaluating projects.
Alignment with European approaches is particularly important as Ukraine pursues EU membership. The country is gradually adapting its regulatory architecture to European standards, including those affecting capital markets and corporate governance.
Ukraine’s Ministry of Economy said clearer rules would help businesses, investors and public institutions apply European sustainable finance standards.
The roadmap also calls for corporate sustainability due diligence. That would bring governance and risk management more directly into investment decisions as Ukraine develops its reconstruction pipeline.
ESG enters public investment management
The government also plans to integrate ESG principles into public investment management.
That could have significant implications for how reconstruction projects are assessed and prioritised. Ukraine will need to balance immediate rebuilding requirements with longer-term climate, environmental and social objectives.
Monitoring sustainable finance flows forms another part of the roadmap. Better tracking could help policymakers understand where sustainable capital is being deployed and identify areas struggling to attract investment.
For investors, credible monitoring could also improve transparency around reconstruction financing.
RELATED ARTICLE: Sony Group Further Supports Humanitarian Relief for Ukraine Emergency
The government plans to develop financial instruments that broaden businesses’ access to capital markets. The roadmap does not specify how much additional financing these measures could mobilise.
Its approval also does not mean the proposed requirements are already in force. Instead, it establishes a framework for further regulatory and institutional development between 2026 and 2028.
That distinction matters. The effectiveness of the initiative will depend on how quickly Ukraine converts the roadmap into workable rules and whether companies can meet the resulting requirements.
Reconstruction finance faces an ESG test
Ukraine’s reconstruction presents an unusual sustainable finance challenge. Capital must support physical rebuilding while also helping modernise infrastructure and strengthen economic resilience.
For international investors, consistent ESG definitions could reduce uncertainty when evaluating projects. A recognised taxonomy may also make it easier to compare Ukrainian opportunities with investments elsewhere in Europe.
Due diligence requirements could strengthen confidence further by establishing clearer expectations for corporate conduct and sustainability risk management.
Yet regulation alone will not unlock investment. Companies will need the systems, data and internal governance required to demonstrate compliance. Public institutions will also need sufficient capacity to monitor implementation.
For executives and investors considering Ukraine’s reconstruction, the roadmap therefore provides direction rather than certainty.
Its longer-term importance will depend on execution. If Ukraine can translate European-aligned ESG principles into credible investment rules, sustainable finance could become an important channel for reconstruction capital. It could also bring the country’s financial architecture closer to the standards expected across the EU.
That would connect Ukraine’s immediate rebuilding needs with a broader economic objective: creating an investment market capable of attracting international capital well beyond the reconstruction period.

articles.title: Opinion: The Constraints Slowing AI Growth will make AI more Sustainable
articles.summary:
AI is advancing at a breakneck pace. Whether that pace is sustainable is perhaps the biggest question facing all of its players. In a recent global survey by Digital Reality, […]
The post Opinion: The Constraints Slowing AI Growth will make AI more Sustainable appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Opinion: The Constraints Slowing AI Growth will make AI more Sustainable
AI is advancing at a breakneck pace. Whether that pace is sustainable is perhaps the biggest question facing all of its players.
In a recent global survey by Digital Reality, a data center services provider, respondents expected their AI spending to increase 32% over the next year. But 40% identified a lack of the necessary infrastructure as the primary restriction on their AI initiatives — up from just 9% in 2024.
A company can deploy a new LLM or expand an AI application relatively quickly (often thanks to AI itself), while adding the physical capacity needed to support it can take years. Data centers depend on available power and water, chips, cooling equipment, transmission infrastructure, permits, and the supply chains required to build and operate them. Those resources cannot scale at the pace of AI adoption.
That mismatch is often framed as a problem to solve: Build more energy generation, expand the grid, add data center capacity, and secure more hardware as fast as possible. That framing is surely driving shifts in community and regulator sentiments.
But constraints can also serve another purpose. They can expose inefficiencies and force companies across what I call the AI ecosystem to make choices about how they use limited resources.
This isn’t bad news. In fact, I believe the infrastructure limitations slowing AI today could be one of the best things to happen for its sustainable development — and the resilience of the AI economy as a whole.
If leaders treat power, water, hardware, regulations, and other constraints as interconnected and interdependent, rather than solving for each one separately, the pressure to keep pace with AI demand can push the entire AI ecosystem toward more efficient and sustainable ways of operating.
Friction forces efficiency
In my role at Sphera, I have a front row seat to the many risks, including safety and sustainability challenges, facing companies across the AI ecosystem. Those challenges are often amplified by the rapid pace of change that’s forcing leaders to keep up with the AI boom.
But companies can’t assume every resource will be available whenever and wherever they need it, which may be frustrating for a CEO trying to scale AI. My view is the constraints above serve as a needed point of friction that forces discipline, leading to better outcomes.
Consider electricity. When power is abundant and inexpensive, there is less pressure to scrutinize how efficiently every watt is used. But when capacity is limited, that scrutiny increases visibility on the impacts of new sources of demand (like EVs and data centers), which in turn leads to new policies and more resilient energy planning.
Along these lines, NVIDIA has promoted AI tokens per watt as a way to measure the amount of useful AI output against the amount of electricity required to produce it. That creates incentives to improve efficiency at multiple levels, from designing chips that deliver more computing power per watt, to developing smaller or compressed AI models that require fewer resources to run. It can also streamline how and when AI models are deployed in the first place.
The same dynamic applies elsewhere. Water constraints can influence cooling technologies and where facilities are built. Scarcity of specialized hardware is a good incentive to extend equipment life and improve utilization. Grid limitations can encourage companies to make more deliberate decisions about where and when compute-intensive workloads run.
I see these pressures as being deeply interconnected. For example, solving for limited power without considering water use could simply shift environmental pressure elsewhere. Likewise, expanding data center capacity without understanding hardware supply chains could create a different constraint downstream.
That’s why AI infrastructure is better understood as an ecosystem in which decisions about one resource, in one part of the ecosystem, can have direct consequences somewhere else.
RELATED ARTICLE: Sphera Adds AI Tools to Turn ESG Data Into Business Value
Acting on constraints makes good business sense
A powerful aspect, before the AI ecosystem argument even enters into it, is much of this is already good business on its own, A supplier managing its own supply chain risk, an operator tracking its own emissions, an enterprise measuring its own AI footprint — each makes sense in pure self-interest.
But because these segments are connected, that work rarely stays contained. A supplier’s better data becomes an operator’s better decision. An operator’s tracked emissions become a utility’s clearer demand signal. Companies acting in their own interest end up helping the peers and partners around them.
To turn constraints into more sustainable and resilient business, a company’s leaders need to know where their biggest dependencies are, and where limitations create opportunities to operate better.
The keys:
- Embrace AI efficiency metrics like tokens per watt. Strategic measures that combine AI outputs with the resources used have the power to reshape behaviors across the ecosystem, while driving better, more sustainable decisions for an individual company.
- Know where your business is vulnerable. Identify the resources and partners your growth depends on most, whether it’s energy, water, chips, suppliers, or data center capacity. Then consider what happens to your business if those resources become harder or more expensive to access.
- Build a complete picture of your impact. Required disclosures won’t necessarily tell you where your biggest risks or tradeoffs are. Tracking energy, water, emissions, and other impacts more closely will help companies better understand how a decision in one area affects another.
- Develop capabilities before a mandate forces the issue. Better supply chain visibility, environmental accounting, and operational risk management can help you make stronger infrastructure decisions today while putting you in a better position to respond to future requirements.
AI’s limits work in our favor
It’s a safe assumption that AI infrastructure will keep expanding, but it will be years before it catches up to demand. Power plants, transmission lines, data centers, and supply chains simply don’t move that fast.
That friction gives companies a reason to get more from the resources they already have. And when companies understand how those resources connect, they can improve efficiency without simply shifting the environmental cost somewhere else.
AI’s limitations are real. Used well, they can also help us build the next phase of AI more sustainably.
By Dan Magestro, Chief Data & AI Officer, Sphera
As Chief Data & AI Officer, Dan Magestro leads Sphera’s data strategy and organization, supporting Sphera’s portfolio of data-driven sustainability and risk solutions. Dan also leads Sphera’s support of the AI economy, connecting Sphera’s products and expertise to the unique needs of companies navigating the AI boom. He has 20+ years of industry and consulting leadership and holds a Ph.D. in nuclear science.

articles.title: European EV Sales Hit Record 1.6 Million as Affordable Models Expand
articles.summary:
Europe’s electric vehicle market is accelerating in 2026 as lower-priced models broaden consumer choice and help automakers close compliance gaps under EU emissions rules. Electric vehicle sales across the European […]
The post European EV Sales Hit Record 1.6 Million as Affordable Models Expand appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
European EV Sales Hit Record 1.6 Million as Affordable Models Expand
- EU electric vehicle sales reached 1.64 million between January and August 2026, up 45% year-on-year and the highest volume recorded for the period.
- EVs captured 22% of the EU car market, six percentage points higher than a year earlier, as manufacturers expanded their electric line-ups to meet emissions targets.
- European automakers account for nearly 60% of available EV models, while Chinese manufacturers hold 21%, intensifying competition across the region’s growing electric vehicle market.
Europe’s electric vehicle market is accelerating in 2026 as lower-priced models broaden consumer choice and help automakers close compliance gaps under EU emissions rules.
Electric vehicle sales across the European Union reached a record 1.64 million between January and August, according to a new report from Transport & Environment (T&E). Sales increased 45% compared with the same period in 2025.
Battery electric vehicles accounted for 22% of the market during the period. That was six percentage points higher than a year earlier.
The Brussels-based environmental group called 2026 “a pivotal year for EV availability”, with the number of models available to European consumers increasing 50% in a single year.
Affordable models reshape the market
The expansion comes as automakers introduce more lower-cost electric vehicles, addressing one of the biggest barriers to wider adoption.
Volkswagen is among the European manufacturers rolling out more affordable models, including the all-electric Polo. The broader product push is helping the German automaker reduce its compliance gap under EU vehicle emissions requirements.
That carries a direct financial consequence. Carmakers that fail to meet mandated fleet emissions levels can face regulatory penalties, making EV sales increasingly important to both climate strategies and balance sheets.
The increase in choice is also changing the competitive landscape.
European manufacturers accounted for nearly 60% of EV models available in the market, according to T&E. They added 16 models during the first half of 2026 alone.
Chinese automakers held a 21% share of available models and added another 11 during the same period.
For European manufacturers, the figures provide evidence that domestic groups are responding to competition from Chinese EV companies. The next test will be whether they can maintain that position as price competition intensifies.
EU emissions rules drive investment decisions
The sales increase comes as European policymakers balance decarbonisation goals with concerns over the competitiveness of the region’s automotive industry.
EU emissions standards have pushed manufacturers to increase the proportion of zero-emission vehicles in their fleets. That pressure is now translating into broader product ranges and greater investment in mass-market models.
The shift has implications beyond vehicle sales.
Automakers must allocate capital across electric platforms, battery supply chains and manufacturing capacity while managing the declining economics of combustion-engine vehicles. Investors are therefore watching EV adoption as both a regulatory compliance issue and an indicator of future competitiveness.
The 45% rise in sales suggests that Europe’s EV transition is increasingly moving beyond premium vehicles and early adopters.
Greater availability at lower price points could accelerate that shift further, particularly as the cost of operating combustion-engine vehicles rises.
RELATED ARTICLE: Walmart Expands EV Charging Network to 100 Stores
Fuel prices strengthen the EV economics
T&E also pointed to higher fuel prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East as another factor affecting consumer economics.
Diesel prices have risen 38% since the Iran war began, according to the report. Filling a 50-litre diesel tank now costs around $34 more than before the conflict.
Higher fuel costs can strengthen the total-cost-of-ownership case for electric vehicles, particularly for drivers with access to lower-cost home charging.
However, affordability remains broader than sticker price alone. Charging infrastructure, electricity costs, financing and access to residential charging will continue to influence adoption across individual European markets.
What executives and investors should watch
Europe’s record EV sales suggest regulation, product availability and consumer economics are beginning to reinforce one another.
For automakers, expanding affordable EV line-ups is increasingly tied to regulatory compliance and market share. For investors, the pace of adoption will shape capital requirements across batteries, manufacturing, charging and automotive supply chains.
The competitive stakes are also growing. European manufacturers currently retain the largest share of EV models available, but Chinese automakers continue to expand their presence.
With EVs already accounting for more than one in five new cars sold across the EU in the first eight months of 2026, Europe’s transition is entering a more commercially consequential phase. The question is shifting from whether consumers will adopt electric vehicles to which manufacturers can compete most effectively as the mass market expands.

articles.title: Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash
articles.summary:
Amazon is committing more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its US data centers. The investment comes as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure faces growing […]
The post Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Amazon Commits $1 Billion to US Data Center Communities Amid AI Backlash
- Amazon will invest more than $1 billion over five years in US communities hosting its data centers, targeting education, workforce training, energy affordability and water preservation.
- AWS says it is 75% of the way toward its 2030 water-positive goal, as scrutiny grows over the electricity and water demands of AI infrastructure.
- More than 100 data center moratoriums are under consideration across the US, raising political and investment risks as technology companies accelerate AI infrastructure spending.
Amazon is committing more than $1 billion over five years to communities hosting its US data centers. The investment comes as the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure faces growing resistance over energy costs, water consumption and local impacts.
Amazon Web Services will direct the funding through its new Built Together framework. It will support education, job training, energy affordability, water preservation and other community priorities.
The initiative adds a community investment component to one of the largest private infrastructure expansions underway in the United States. Amazon said it invested $276 billion in data centers between 2011 and 2025.
Large projects or expansions are now underway across several states, including Indiana, Louisiana, North Carolina, Virginia and Mississippi.
AI growth collides with local infrastructure concerns
Data centers provide the computing capacity required to train and operate AI models. Their rapid expansion has also intensified questions about who bears the infrastructure costs.
Communities across the US have raised concerns about electricity demand, utility bills, water use and pressure on local infrastructure. More than 100 data center moratoriums are currently being considered nationwide, according to Amazon.
That opposition creates a growing governance challenge for technology companies and policymakers. It also adds a political dimension ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
AWS CEO Matt Garman framed continued construction as an economic and national security priority.
“There is urgency to this data center buildout because we aren’t the only country that sees the benefits of AI for the economy and national security, and the countries that lead in AI will shape it and get the most from it,” Garman said.
Amazon compared the current expansion of digital infrastructure with the construction of the US interstate highway system. However, the company stressed one major difference. Private companies, rather than taxpayers, are financing much of today’s infrastructure buildout.
AI infrastructure is increasingly tied to healthcare, education, financial services, cybersecurity, defense and scientific research. That broadening role has strengthened the case for investment while increasing scrutiny of its environmental footprint.
RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany
Water and energy move higher on the agenda
Amazon’s investment framework seeks to address some of the most contentious environmental issues surrounding data centers.
AWS has committed to becoming water positive across its data center operations by 2030. The company said it is now 75% of the way toward that goal. Water positive means returning more water to communities than its operations consume.
The commitment has become increasingly relevant as new data centers expand into regions facing competing demands for water and electricity.
Energy affordability is another focus of the $1 billion program. Rising data center demand has prompted questions about grid investment and whether households could face higher costs as utilities build infrastructure to serve large technology customers.
For Amazon, addressing those concerns has become part of maintaining community support for continued expansion.
Community acceptance becomes an investment risk
The scale of proposed data center development means community relations are moving from corporate philanthropy into core infrastructure strategy.
Moratoriums, permitting disputes and public opposition can delay projects and raise development costs. They can also complicate the long-term power procurement and grid planning needed to support AI investment.
Amazon’s Built Together framework gives communities a role in determining how funds are allocated. That approach could help companies align investments with local concerns rather than applying a uniform national model.
For executives and investors, the broader issue extends beyond Amazon. AI growth depends on physical infrastructure that requires land, power, water and political approval.
The next phase of the AI investment cycle will therefore depend on more than access to capital and computing technology. Developers will need credible plans for resource use, community benefits and energy affordability.
As governments compete for leadership in AI, those local constraints are becoming part of the global race for digital infrastructure. The companies that manage them effectively may gain an advantage in securing the permits, power and public support required for continued expansion.
